attributes.title: Level 3

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you flip the Player sprite’s image asset vertically and give it a descriptive name?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How might the Player sprite’s upside down image asset be used in the project?

❓ What does the flip vertical tool do in the paint editor? Why might it be useful?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja how that they can duplicate an asset by clicking on it, then selecting Duplicate from the left side menu. Once duplicated, remind the ninja to open the new asset to edit it, then revise its name. 


💡 The flip vertical tool flips an image vertically, creating an upside down version. This is useful when a sprite faces different directions in a project.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by creating multiple Player sprite image assets to be used throughout the project!


Click the Assets menu along the top of the screen, and notice the images, tiles, and tilemap stored in My Assets. Then, create a new image asset for the Player sprite and give it a descriptive name. 


Once created, duplicate the Player sprite’s original image and edit the new asset. Use the flip vertical tool in the top left of the paint editor, to create an upside down version of the Player sprite’s image. Give the new asset a descriptive name.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type assets, a dot operator, and the asset type, followed by the name of the asset inside 2 backticks `` in the tilemap parameter?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What function should be used to display a tilemap on screen?

❓ Where should the name of the tilemap be typed in the setCurrentTilemap function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja to check the documentation if they need help displaying adding a background color or displaying a tilemap on screen.
steps.instructions:
Set a background color and display a tilemap on screen!


Return to the JavaScript editor, then add a // game initialization comments at the top. Underneath, set the background color and the tilemap from My Assets.


Click ▶ to see the tilemap appear on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you edit the vx and vy parameters of the moveSprite function so the Player sprite can only move horizontally?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code should be added inside the spriteImage array’s brackets so that it contains the Player sprite’s 2 image assets?

❓ What index should be used from the spriteImage array to set the Player sprite’s image?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that when calling an asset in their code, they need to type assets, a dot operator, the asset type, and the name of the asset inside 2 backticks ``. This should be done for each of the Player sprite’s image assets and they should be separated by a comma between the array’s brackets.

💡 Encourage the ninja to use documentation if they need assistance coding the Player sprite to move with direction buttons, setting it to stay in screen, or setting the camera to follow it.
steps.instructions:
Add a Player sprite to the project!


Create a spriteImage array under // game initialization to store the two Player sprite image assets. Inside the brackets, type the names of both image assets from My Assets, separated by a comma.


Below, add a Player sprite to the project. Set the Player sprite’s image to the index of the original image asset in the spriteImage array.


Add code to move the Player sprite horizontally (right and left) around the tilemap with direction buttons. 


Then, set the camera to follow the Player sprite.


Click ▶ to test the Player sprite’s movement!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the Player sprite’s y-acceleration to the spriteAcceleration variable?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might the Player sprite’s y-acceleration be stored in the spriteAcceleration variable? 

❓ Why does the Player sprite’s y-acceleration need to be set in a 2D platformer tilemap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In this project, the Player sprite’s gravity will be “flipped”, which means an opposite y-acceleration value will be applied to the Player sprite. This will cause the Player sprite to move upside down. By storing the sprite’s y-acceleration in a variable, the value can easily be updated throughout the project.
steps.instructions:
Add gravity to the Player sprite’s movement!


Declare a spriteAcceleration variable set to 200 underneath // game initialization.


Below the Player sprite’s code, use the Player sprite’s name and a dot operator to set the y-acceleration (ay) to the spriteAcceleration variable.


Click ▶ to test what happens when the Player sprite moves off of a platform on the tilemap.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you check if !upsideDown inside the if condition?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What might happen when the user presses the A button?

❓ How is the Boolean NOT operator ! used to check if the upsideDown variable is not true?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that the Boolean NOT operator ! is useful for checking if a Boolean variable is false. Explain to the ninja that !upsideDown is the same as upsideDown == false. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to use documentation if they need assistance declaring the upsideDown variable or adding a Boolean NOT operator !.
steps.instructions:
“Flip” the gravity when the user presses the A button.


Underneath // game initialization, declare an upsideDown variable set to false.


Below the Player sprite’s code, add a // game events comment and an A button pressed event underneath. 


Add an if/else conditional inside the A button pressed event. Check if the upsideDown variable is not true in the if condition, using a Boolean NOT operator !.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use * to multiply the sprite’s y-acceleration?
steps.senseiHelp:
﻿Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens if the upsideDown variable is not true when the onEvent function runs?

❓ Why is the sprite’s y-acceleration multiplied by -1 to flip its gravity?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 If the upsideDown variable is not true when the onEvent function runs, upsideDown will be set to true, the sprite’s image will be changed to the upside down image asset, the sprite’s y-acceleration will be multiplied by -1, and a new background color will be set.

💡 Prompt the ninja to consider why multiplying the sprite’s y-acceleration by -1 will cause its gravity to flip. When a positive value is multiplied by -1, it becomes a negative value. This causes the sprite’s acceleration to move in the opposite direction, making the sprite float up instead of being pulled down.
steps.instructions:
Change the Player sprite’s image and properties when gravity is flipped!


Inside the controller.A event, if the Player sprite is !upsideDown when the flipGravity function is called, set the variable to true. 


Then, use the spriteImage array to set the Player sprite’s image to the upside down image asset. 


Change the Player sprite’s  y-acceleration (ay) to the value of the spriteAcceleration variable multiplied by -1, to pull the sprite to the top of the screen.


Last, change the background color in the if condition when gravity is flipped.


Click ▶ to test what happens when the A button is pressed!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you change the value of the upsideDown variable, then reset the sprite’s image and y-acceleration if upsideDown is true?
steps.senseiHelp:
﻿Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the A button is pressed, if upsideDown is true?

❓ Does the sprite’s image and y-acceleration flip correctly when the A button is pressed?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 If the upsideDown variable is true when the A button is pressed, upsideDown will be set to false, the sprite’s image will be changed to the original image asset, the sprite’s y-acceleration will be reset to a positive value, and the original background color will be set.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the project by moving the Player sprite around the tilemap, then pressing the A button repeatedly to ensure that the sprite’s image and y-acceleration change and revert back correctly.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! Once the Player sprite is flipped, it’s stuck upside down!


Inside the A button pressed event, use the else condition to reverse the Player sprite’s direction if the upsideDown variable is true.


Inside the else condition, set the upsideDown variable to false and change the Player sprite’s image to the regular sprite image asset from the spriteImage array. 


Set the y-acceleration back to the positive value of the spriteAcceleration variable. Then change the background color back to the original color.


Click ▶ to test how the Player sprite’s image and gravity changes each time the A button is pressed!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the run condition expression in the for loop so that it runs while the counter variable is less than 10?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What should the run condition expression be set to so that 10 Food sprites are created in the for loop?

❓ What happens when the setCandy function is called?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to use documentation if they need assistance updating the run condition in the for loop.

💡 When the setCandy function is called, 10 Food sprites will appear on random cloudTile assets on the tilemap.
steps.instructions:
Create Food sprites for the Player sprite to collect around the tilemap!


Define a setCandy function under // game initialization.


Add a for loop inside the function definition that will create 10 Food sprites.


Inside the for loop, create a Food sprite using the candy image asset from My Assets. Place each Food sprite on a random cloudTile on the tilemap.


Call the setCandy function under // game initialization below the Player sprite’s code.


Click ▶ to see Food sprites appear on some of the cloudTile tiles across the tilemap.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you update the parameters in the runMovementAnimation function to modify the Food sprite’s animation?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What should the parameters in the runMovementAnimation function be set to so that the Food sprites’ bob in place every 2000ms?

❓ Do the Food sprites’ animation appear correctly on screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can delete .flyToCenter, retype the dot operator, then select bobbing to update the pathString parameter. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out the animation code, then update the parameters if the effect is not appearing correctly.
steps.instructions:
Animate the Food sprites on the tilemap!


Open Animation and drag [animate (mySprite) with (pathString) for (ms) (2000) loop (loop)] inside the for loop. Use the Food sprite’s name in the sprite parameter. Then, update the other parameters to set the sprite’s movement animation to bob continuously every 2000ms.


Click ▶ to test the Food sprite animation code, then adjust the parameters as needed.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use an increment operator ++ to increase the value of candyCount by 1?
steps.senseiHelp:
﻿Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the Player sprite overlaps a Food sprite?

❓ What symbol should be used to increase the candyCount by 1?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the Player sprite overlaps a Food sprite, the Food sprite is destroyed and the candyCount increases by 1.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can type the name of the variable and an increment operator ++, to increase the value of the variable by 1.
steps.instructions:
Make something happen when the Player sprite overlaps a Food sprite!


Declare a candyCount variable set to 0 under // game initialization. 


Create an onOverlap event with the Player and Food sprite kinds under // game events. 


Whenever the Player sprite overlaps with a Food sprite, destroy the Food sprite, then increase the value of candyCount by 1.


Click ▶ to try to collect all of the Food sprites on the tilemap by flipping the gravity to float up and down!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the allOfKind function to check the length of the array of Food sprites?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code should be used inside the parentheses of the if conditional, to check if there are no Food sprites when the Player sprite overlaps a Food sprite?

❓ What sprite kind should be used in the allOfKind function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to use documentation if they need assistance locating the allOfKind function. Remind the ninja to type a dot operator and select the length property after the function.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can use the  setGameOverEffect function before the gameOver function to set an effect to play when the game over screen appears.
steps.instructions:
End the game once all of the Food sprites have been collected!


Add an if conditional inside the onOverlap event to check if the length of the array of Food sprites is equal to 0.


Inside the conditional, add a splash screen that tells the user that they collected all of the candy. Then set the game to end in a win, adding an optional effect to the win screen.


Click ▶ to test out the win condition.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the location parameter in the tileAtLocationEquals function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the Player sprite hits a spikeTileUp wall tile? What happens if it hits any other type of wall tile?

❓ What code should be added to the right of the equality operator == to retrieve the spikeTileUp tile asset?

 ❓What symbol should be used to concatenate a string with the candyCount variable in the splash function?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the Player sprite hits a wall tile, the splash screen will only show if the tile image is a spikeTileUp tile asset. In any other instance, the splash screen will not appear.

💡 Remind the ninja that when calling an asset in their code, they need to type assets, a dot operator, the asset type, and the name of the asset inside 2 backticks ``. 

💡 Encourage the ninja to use documentation if they need assistance concatenating a string with the candyCount variable in the splash function.
steps.instructions:
Add a challenge to the project with hazard tiles!


Open Scene and drag [run code on (sprite) of kind (kind) hits wall at (location)] under // game events.


Add an if conditional inside the onHitWall event, then open Scene and drag [tile at (location) is (tile)] inside the parentheses. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 


tiles.tileAtLocationEquals(tiles.getTile

Location(0, 0), img``)


The tileAtLocationEquals function takes 2 parameters: location and tile image. 


Replace tiles.getTileLocation(0, 0) with the location parameter from the onHitWall event. Replace img`` with the spikeTileUp tile asset.


Add a splash screen inside the event. Concatenate the candyCount variable with a string to tell the user how many Food sprites they collected.


Click ▶ to test what happens when the Player sprite hits a spikeTileUp tile.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use a Boolean OR operator || to check for both  hazard tile images?
steps.senseiHelp:
Note: the entire if condition should be on a single line; it is only shown across 2 lines in the screenshot above to make it easier to read.


Ask the ninja:

❓ What symbol should be used to add a Boolean OR operator inside the parentheses of the if conditional?

❓ What happens when the Player sprite hits a spikeTileUp OR spikeTileDown wall tile? What happens if it hits any other type of wall tile?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja that the ninja that 2 vertical lines || can be used to add a Boolean OR operator to their code.

💡 Now, when the Player sprite hits a wall tile, the splash screen will only show if the tile image is a spikeTileUp OR spikeTileDown tile asset. In any other instance, the splash screen will not appear.

💡 Prompt the ninja to test out their code by overlapping both types of “hazard” tiles, to ensure the condition is functioning properly.
steps.instructions:
Check for a second hazard tile image!


Inside the conditional in the onHitWall event, use a Boolean OR operator to check for a second tile image. 


Copy the entire condition, then paste it to the right of the Boolean OR operator. Change the tile asset to the spikeTileDown tile asset from My Assets.


Click ▶ to test what happens when the Player sprite hits either a spikeTileUp tile or a spikeTileDown tile.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you reassign the variables to their initial values in the startGame function?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What does it mean to initialize a game?

❓ What values will each of the variables be set to when the startGame function is called?

❓ What values might be used in the placeOnTile function, so that the Player sprite appears on a tile at the bottom of the tilemap?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The ninja has already practiced initialization in many ways. Setting variables to a specific value at the beginning of the project creates a starting point that can be updated later. In this example, the variables are declared outside of the startGame function so they are global and can be accessed throughout, but their values are set inside the function. This allows the game to be replayed, without the user having to start completely over and read the directions each time.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can use their cursor to hover over a specific tile, then find its coordinates in the bottom left corner of the tilemap editor.
steps.instructions:
Create a function to initialize the game!


Define a startGame function underneath // game initialization.


Cut and paste the code that sets the tilemap and background color at the beginning of the project, into the function definition.


Then, set the initial, or starting values of the upsideDown and candyCount variables using the same values as the beginning of the project.


Use the spriteImage array to set the Player sprite’s image to the original sprite image asset.


Cut and paste the code that sets the Player sprite’s y-acceleration into the function definition. Then place the Player sprite on a tile at the bottom of the tilemap in the function definition.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you call the startGame function under // game start and inside the conditional in the onHitWall event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is the startGame function called at the beginning of the project and after the Player sprite overlaps a hazard tile?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 The startGame function is called at the beginning of the project to initialize each of the variable values and after the Player sprite overlaps a hazard tile, so that the user can continue to play without having to read the directions again.

💡 Prompt the ninja to test out the project and notice what happens to the Food sprites when the project resets.
steps.instructions:
Call the function to start the game, then again to reset the Player and Food sprites after overlapping a hazard tile.


Cut and paste the setCandy function call under // game initialization into the startGame function definition. 


Then, add a // game start comment, and call the startGame function underneath, as well as inside the conditional in the onHitWall event.


Click ▶ to test out the startGame function.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you destroy all of the existing Food sprites before new Food sprites are created in the setCandy function for loop?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why do Food sprites continue to stay on the screen, even after the project is reset?

❓ Why is the destroyAllSpritesOfKind function useful? How else have you performed this action before?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Prompt the ninja to notice that because new Food sprites are created each time the startGame function is called, existing sprites that weren’t collected in the previous round remain on the screen. This allows the user to collect more than 10 Food sprites. The destroyAllSpritesOfKind function solves this bug by resetting the number of Food sprites each time the project resets.

💡 The destroyAllSpritesOfKind function is useful for resetting the number of sprites of a certain kind on screen. This could also be achieved by using a for element of loop to destroy each element in the array of Food sprites.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! Food sprites continue to stay on the screen, even after the project is reset. 


Open Sprites and drag [destroy all sprites of kind (kind)] to the top of the setCandy function definition.


Click ▶ to see only 10 Food sprites appear on the tilemap when the project is reset.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the marquee tool to select and resize the cursor image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What image might be used for the dialog frame?

❓ How can an image be resized in the paint editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:


💡 Encourage the ninja to use the marquee tool in the paint editor to resize the cursor image.
steps.instructions:
Add instructions to the beginning of the project!


Below // game start, set the dialog frame and dialog cursor below the startGame function call. 


Create 2 new image assets in My Assets: one to be used for the dialog frame, and a duplicated, larger version of the candy sprite image to be used for the dialog cursor. Give both assets a descriptive name, then call the assets in the setDialogFrame and setDialogCursor functions.


Then, create a dialog box to share instructions for the project with the user.


Click ▶ to play the completed project!

subgroups.title: Gravity Jumper
subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses y-acceleration to change a sprite’s movement on a 2D platformer tilemap.

validationItems.text: Display a tilemap asset on screen.
Declare a spriteImage array to store the Player sprite’s images. Create a Player sprite using an image from the array, and set the camera to follow it.
Declare spriteAcceleration and upsideDown variables and assign them initial values.
Use an A button pressed event with an if/else conditional to flip the Player sprite’s gravity, depending on the value of the upsideDown variable.
Create a setCandy function that destroys all of the existing Food sprites, then uses a for loop to create new ones. Call the function inside the startGame function.
Check if the tile image at the location where the Player sprite hits a wall is one of two hazard tiles. If so, call the startGame function to reset the game.
Use a startGame function to initialize and reset the values of variables and the Player sprite.
Use image assets in the dialog frame and cursor image functions.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 3 of Brown Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about using physics and Boolean values to control game conditions in 2D platform tilemap projects. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 3:

badges.title: Taking Control
badges.description: Control the way sprites move and appear on screen in a 2D tilemap project in JavaScript.

badges.title: Gravity of the Situation
badges.description: Use physics to control a sprite’s velocity and acceleration in a 2D tilemap project in JavaScript.

badges.title: Checkin’ it Twice
badges.description: Check for a specific tile image at a specific tilemap location.

badges.title: While You’re At It…
badges.description: Use a while loop to make something happen while a certain condition is true.

badges.title: And the Winner Is…
badges.description: Create a function that uses Boolean operators and values to determine which sprite image to use.

badges.title: Well-Rounded Character
badges.description: Edit an image asset to create multiple versions of an image that faces different directions.
